title: Building Interactive UIs in VS Code with MCP Apps — Marlene Mhangami & Liam Hampton, GitHub

primary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The entire talk focuses on MCP (Model Context Protocol) and how MCP apps enable interactive tool calling and UI rendering. The tools discussed, such as VS Code and GitHub Copilot, are developer platforms used by software builders. The protocol is actively used by companies like Shopify in production while also serving as a framework for building new prototypes. The speakers introduce MCP from basic concepts and include a straightforward live demo suitable for beginners. The presentation is a conference talk that includes live demonstrations of the technology. Multiple direct quotes from the transcript explicitly support the classification into the MCP protocol category.

summary: Marlene Mhangami and Liam Hampton introduce MCP apps, a mechanism for rendering interactive UIs directly inside VS Code chat. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol created by Anthropic that standardizes how applications provide context—tools, prompts, or resources—to LLMs. The architecture has three parts: hosts (programs like VS Code wanting data), clients (maintaining one-to-one server connections, e.g., GitHub Copilot), and servers (lightweight programs exposing capabilities via MCP). A key early limitation of MCP was that it could only return text—ASCII art and emoji-laden readmes were common workarounds. MCP apps solve this by letting server tools return rich interactive components rendered in a sandboxed iframe. The flow: user sends a prompt, the LLM selects an MCP tool, the server returns tool results with a UI resource reference pointing to bundled HTML, the host fetches and renders it in a sandboxed iframe, and the app can call back to the server for fresh data. The sandboxed iframe is critical for security—it prevents the app from interacting with VS Code settings, calling external APIs, or accessing anything outside the chat window, compared using the metaphor of putting a hamster in a cage so it cannot chew things up. Use cases include data exploration (interacting with databases via UI instead of typing), e-commerce (Shopify building full checkout experiences in chat), architecture diagrams (Excalidraw), and component generation (Figma). Liam demos a flame graph MCP app profiling a Go program with bubble sort and Fibonacci algorithms over 5 seconds using Go pprof, built from an edited skill from the MCP repository run through GitHub Copilot CLI. The demo shows GitHub Copilot automatically recognizing and calling the flame graph profiler tool, rendering an interactive UI in the chat window showing top functions and a summary of where time is spent, eliminating the need for back-and-forth questioning of AI models about performance data. The app has three parts: the tool (LLM + host), the resource (bundled HTML UI, in React using hooks), and the link between them. The demo repository also includes markdown viewer, flight status, and color picker apps. The talk closes with invitations to visit the GitHub booth and Microsoft Build (June 3-6).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Marlene Mhangami and Liam Hampton introduce themselves as senior developer advocates at Microsoft/GitHub. They outline the agenda: what MCP is, why MCP apps are needed, what they are, and live demos by Liam.

sections.title: MCP Overview
sections.summary: MCP is an open protocol created by Anthropic standardizing how applications provide context to LLMs. The architecture includes hosts (VS Code), clients (GitHub Copilot), and servers (lightweight programs). VS Code recommends using servers from its extensions tab for security.

sections.title: Why MCP Apps and How They Work
sections.summary: Early MCP returned only text (ASCII art, emojis). MCP apps let server tools return rich interactive components rendered in sandboxed iframes. The flow: user prompt, LLM selects tool, server returns data with UI resource reference, host fetches HTML, renders in sandboxed iframe, app calls back to server for fresh data.

sections.title: MCP App Use Cases
sections.summary: Use cases include data exploration (interacting with databases via UI), e-commerce (Shopify building checkout experiences in chat preserving brand feel), Excalidraw for interactive architecture diagrams, and Figma for generating components on the fly.

sections.title: Live Demo Setup
sections.summary: Liam demonstrates building MCP apps from a skill on the MCP repository, edited and run through GitHub Copilot CLI. An MCP app has three parts: tool (LLM + host), resource (bundled HTML UI), and the link between them. Demo uses a Go file with bubble sort and Fibonacci, profiled over 5 seconds with Go pprof, rendered as a flame graph in a React app using hooks.

sections.title: Live Demo Execution and Iframe Security
sections.summary: Liam shows GitHub Copilot automatically recognizing and calling the flame graph profiler tool, rendering an interactive UI in the chat window showing top functions and time-spent summary. The UI can be edited and resized to fit the chat window, eliminating back-and-forth questioning of AI models about performance. Liam revisits the flow: profile command to LLM, tool call, MCP server returns JSON, host recognizes resource link, renders in iframe. The sandboxed iframe prevents the app from interacting with VS Code settings or external APIs—compared to putting a hamster in a cage so it cannot chew things up.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Marlene and Liam close by inviting attendees to visit the GitHub booth and mentioning Microsoft Build (June 3-6) focusing on code with workshops, available online as well.
